summary.text: Assuming either family finite, bound its representatives by \(B\) and apply the decomposition hypothesis to \(n=(B+3)!\), writing \(6n=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\). In the Sophie Germain case \(6x-1\) divides the factorial, while in the twin-prime case the bound on \(6y-1\) makes \(6y+1\) divide it; each therefore divides the prime on the opposite side of the displayed sum, forcing equality (or divisibility by 1), both impossible since the two numbers are prime and are incongruent modulo \(6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{t\in\mathbb N:t\text{ is prime and }t+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs. Thus infinitude of \(T\) is precisely infinitude of twin-prime pairs, since each \(t\in T\) represents the pair \((t,t+2)\).

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(A227923(n)\) is the sum, over integers \(x\) satisfying \(1\le x<n\), of the indicator of the following condition. Put
\[
y=n-x.
\]
Then
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Because \(x\ge 1\),
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say exactly that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. The last two say that \((6y-1,6y+1)\) is a twin-prime pair.

Assume throughout that
\[
A227923(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We first record the direct consequence of positivity that will be used in both parts of the proof. Since \(A227923(n)\) is a finite sum of terms, each of which is either \(0\) or \(1\), positivity of this sum implies that at least one term is \(1\). Consequently, for every \(n>1\), there are integers \(x,y\ge 1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Indeed, the relevant summation index satisfies \(1\le x<n\), and hence \(y=n-x\ge1\). In particular, for every such decomposition we have the important identity
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n. \tag{1}
\]

We now prove separately that \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite.

### Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(S\) is finite. Every finite set of natural numbers is bounded above, so choose an integer \(B\ge0\) such that
\[
p\le B\qquad\text{for every }p\in S. \tag{2}
\]
Set
\[
n=(B+3)!.
\]
Since \(B+3\ge3\), its factorial is at least \(3\), and therefore \(n>1\). By the assumed positivity of \(A227923(n)\), choose \(x,y\ge1\), with \(x+y=n\), such that the four numbers above are prime.

Put
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad q=6y+1.
\]
The number \(p\) is prime, and
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime. Hence \(p\in S\). By (2), \(p\le B\), and in particular
\[
1\le p\le B+3.
\]
Every positive integer at most \(B+3\) divides \((B+3)!\), because it occurs as one of the factors in that factorial. Thus
\[
p\mid (B+3)!=n,
\]
and consequently
\[
p\mid 6n. \tag{3}
\]

On the other hand, identity (1) says
\[
p+q=6n.
\]
Since \(p\mid 6n\) and of course \(p\mid p\), subtracting gives
\[
p\mid q. \tag{4}
\]
But \(q=6y+1\) is prime. A positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself. The divisor \(p\) cannot be \(1\), because \(p\) is prime. Therefore (4) forces
\[
p=q.
\]
This is impossible: modulo \(6\), one has
\[
p=6x-1\equiv -1\equiv5\pmod 6,
\qquad
q=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6.
\]
Equality would therefore imply \(5\equiv1\pmod6\), which is false. This contradiction shows that \(S\) cannot be finite. Hence there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.

### Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Suppose instead, for a contradiction, that \(T\) is finite. Again choose an integer \(B\ge0\) bounding all its elements:
\[
t\le B\qquad\text{for every }t\in T. \tag{5}
\]
As before, set
\[
n=(B+3)!>1.
\]
The positivity hypothesis supplies integers \(x,y\ge1\), with \(x+y=n\), for which
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime.

Write
\[
t=6y-1,
\qquad
q=6y+1=t+2,
\qquad
p=6x-1.
\]
Both \(t\) and \(t+2=q\) are prime, so \(t\in T\). The bound (5) gives
\[
t=6y-1\le B.
\]
It follows that
\[
q=t+2\le B+2\le B+3. \tag{6}
\]
The number \(q\) is prime and hence positive. From (6), it is a positive integer no larger than \(B+3\), so it divides \((B+3)!\). Therefore
\[
q\mid n
\quad\text{and hence}\quad
q\mid 6n. \tag{7}
\]

Using identity (1) once more, now in the form
\[
p+q=6n,
\]
we see from (7), together with \(q\mid q\), that
\[
q\mid p. \tag{8}
\]
The number \(p=6x-1\) is prime. Thus every positive divisor of \(p\) is either \(1\) or \(p\). Since \(q\) is itself prime, it is not \(1\); hence (8) implies
\[
q=p.
\]
Again this is impossible modulo \(6\), because
\[
q=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6,
\qquad
p=6x-1\equiv5\pmod6.
\]
This contradiction proves that \(T\) is infinite, and therefore that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

We have proved both conclusions: if \(A227923(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\), then there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
